newsitem.title: USA: Simpson broke and can't pay bills, jury told.
newsitem.headline: Simpson broke and can't pay bills, jury told.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial who will decide whether to impose punitive damages on the former football star were told Friday he is unable to earn any money and is struggling to pay his bills.
Leroy "Skip" Taft, Simpson's business manager, said Simpson's earning capacity was nil and his future prospects were bleak.
The jury Tuesday blamed Simpson for the murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, and awarded $8.5 million in damages to Goldman's divorced parents.

The plaintiffs in the wrongful death trial want the jury to punish him further by awarding millions more to the estates of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman. Jurors could begin deliberating the matter by Friday afternoon.
Taft gave the jurors a glimpse of what it costs to live in the world of the rich and famous, listing Simpson's considerable monthly expenses.
He said the mortgage on Simpson's mansion in the posh Brentwood section of Los Angeles was $24,000 and month "when he pays it," and the cost of maintaining the estate was about $30,000 a month.

In addition, Taft said in answer to questions from plaintiffs' attorney Peter Gelblum, he charged the former athlete about $10,000 a month for his services; Simpson pays his personal secretary $3,000 a month and employs a full-time bodyguard, whose salary was not disclosed.
Simpson, who was not in court for the final phase of his trial, also recently bought a $54,000 Chevrolet Suburban and owns a Bentley valued at between $35,000 and $40,000, Taft said.
He also told the jury Simpson owes him thousands of dollars in unpaid fees that he did not expect to ever receive. "He has to pay his bills selectively," Taft said.

Taft said Simpson's recent efforts to exploit his name had met with no success. Promoters of sports memorabilia shows refused to have Simpson at their events, and the only promoter who did accept him for an Atlanta show cancelled the appearance after receiving bomb threats.
He said it was "ludicrous" to say that Simpson could earn $2.5 million a year selling his name and likeness, as a plaintiffs' witness testified Thursday.
